title: Ida Oppaan ajankohtainen notaarintutkielma palkittiin maailman parhaana
content:
The award-winning thesis, The Relationship Between Company-level Collective Agreements and European Union Competition Law, was completed under the supervision of Associate Professor Jari Murto.

The victory came as a pleasant surprise to Opas.

“I’d received a good grade for my thesis and the supervisor gave me really good feedback, so I thought I’d try out how I’d fare in an international competition. I thought maybe I could receive some small recognition there. When they called and told me that I’d won the entire category, I was really surprised.” 

Opas’s thesis examines the relationship between company-level collective agreements and EU competition law. The topic is particularly important, since company-level agreements remain on the rise in Finland.

In her thesis, Opas investigates whether Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), the central competition provision of EU law, applies to company-level collective agreements, or whether they are excluded from the review of competition law in the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union in the same way as traditional collective agreements.

title: Prof. Van Berkel visits HELICS as a North America Research Fellow
content:
Derek Van Berkel, Associate Professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, is joining the University of Helsinki for a research sabbatical as a North America Research Fellow, in collaboration with Professor Enrico Di Minin at the Helsinki Lab of Interdisciplinary Conservation Science (HELICS). His research combines geospatial data science, participatory mapping, and artificial intelligence to understand human–environment interactions and support environmental planning and decision-making.

During his stay, Van Berkel will collaborate with HELICS researchers to investigate how digital data, particularly social media, can help detect changes in visitation, recreation, and other human activities following landscape change. The collaboration brings together expertise in conservation science, biodiversity, GeoAI, and participatory geographic information systems to develop innovative approaches for understanding landscape change and supporting evidence-based environmental decision-making.

title: Kenttäjakso Satakunnassa: intensiivinen viikko käytännön kokemusta ja yritysyhteistyötä
content:
In the Faculty of Agriculture and Forestry’s international master's programme, Technologies for Sustainable Use of Renewable Resources, students complete studies in the Satakunta region in Western Finland in addition to the Viikki campus. In the 2026–2027 academic year, four field weeks will be held in the region, the first of which took place on 19–23 October 2026. During these weeks, students are introduced to the operations of the food and forestry sectors and learn how to apply emerging technologies and sustainable solutions in practice. 

The group's journey began early on Monday morning as they departed Viikki by bus for Satakunta. On the way, they stopped in Jokioinen at Elonkierto to learn about research on natural resources in the park. The day continued in Rauma, where the students visited the SAMK campus and finalised their group pitches for Tuesday.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: HIKET at Climate Currents: Looking ahead to COP31
content:
HIKET project took part in the Climate Currents event “What to expect for COP31?”, organized by University of Helsinki and Aalto University at Tiedekulma on 27 October. The event brought together researchers, policymakers, business representatives and young people to explore the key issues ahead of COP31 and the wider COP process.

HIKET’s objectives for COP31, presented by Research Director Tuomo Kalliokoski, include developing wider research cooperation to support land-sector climate decisions at the global level.  

Another key objective is connecting research with climate action. HIKET research bridges the gap between science, policy and business, which supports implementation of the Paris Agreement.  

Reliable evidence for effective AFOLU mitigation actions ensures engagement of policymakers and creates new opportunities for business applications.

The desired outcome: shared interest, identified partners and agreed next steps.

title: HIKET in Brussels: Towards an EU-wide integrated approach to LULUCF monitoring
content:
Reliable and transparent information on carbon sinks and emissions is essential for effective climate policy. Yet significant uncertainties remain, and differences in national monitoring and modelling approaches make comparisons across Europe challenging.

The HIKET approach offers a potential way forward: integrating ground-based observations, satellite data, inventories and multiple modelling approaches into a common framework for independent verification, uncertainty assessment and policy-relevant scenario analysis. Building on existing European research infrastructures, this could provide a foundation for a more coherent and reliable EU-wide LULUCF monitoring system.

Many thanks to ForestNavigator EU project, The Directorate-General for Climate Action (DG CLIMA, European Commission), Open Geospatial Carbon Registry (OGCR) project & Project CAFAMORE for the invitations and the opportunity to exchange ideas and explore future collaboration!

title: Guest lecture: Teaching difficult history in a polarized age, 19.11.2026
content:
How can we teach difficult history in a world increasingly divided by political conflicts, social media, and competing narratives? And how can Holocaust and genocide education help students develop the critical thinking skills needed to navigate a polarized society?

In an age of misinformation, echo chambers, and growing social divisions, teaching history is more important—and more challenging—than ever. While public debates often encourage simple answers and clear-cut distinctions between “us” and “them,” history education demands careful analysis, evidence-based reasoning, and a willingness to engage with different perspectives.

Drawing on twenty years of experience in Holocaust and genocide education in Denmark, Danish Holocaust educator Solvej Berlau explores the challenges and possibilities of teaching difficult history today. The lecture examines the development of Holocaust and genocide education in Denmark, including its introduction as a compulsory subject in 2023, and addresses a fundamental question: What does it mean not only to learn about the Holocaust and other genocides, but also to learn from them?

title: Lucia Cerullo’s Elamite Metalworks, Part 1
content:
Dr. Lucia Cerullo is an archaeologist and art historian with a PhD in Asia, Africa, and the Mediterraneum from the University of Naples “L’Orientale”, in Italy. Her academic path began with a focus on Elamite epigraphy, explored in her Bachelor’s thesis on royal inscriptions from Persepolis. Over time, she developed a dual focus in archaeology and epigraphy, which she sees as essential in fully understanding ancient cultures. She has worked as an archaeologist in Italy, and held senior roles in fieldwork across Uzbekistan and Iran, including nearly seven years at the Iran National Museum in Tehran. Her expertise focuses on 1st Millenium BCE material culture, especially metal objects and pottery. 

Can you tell us something about the book to start off?

It is a catalogue of metal vessels that focuses on three collections: Arǧān, Ǧūbaǧī, and Kalmākarrah. Two of them are burials, Arǧān and Ǧūbaǧī, while Kalmākarrah is a hoard, or treasure, found inside a cave. The descriptions of the collections include the problems they present, a bit of research history, and the discovery context.
